- When sentiment is strongly negative (e.g., < -0.5) in recent days, model tends to overcorrect upward — reduce forecast peak by 5–10%.
- After a sharp price spike, model often overshoots and fails to correct — dampen forecast slope downward for 3–5 days post-spike.
- If sentiment is neutral or mildly positive (0.0–0.3), model tends to overestimate mean reversion — adjust downward by 2–5% for 2–4 days.
- Model consistently overestimates short-term (1–7 day) declines when sentiment is negative — apply upward bias to forecast for 1–3 days.
- When sentiment is positive and price is falling, model often underestimates the drop — increase forecast downward by 3–7% for 2–5 days.
- Model underestimates long-term (10+ day) mean reversion when sentiment is negative — add 2–5% upward bias for 5–7 days.
- If sentiment is consistently negative over 3+ days, model tends to forecast a “bottom” too early — delay downward forecast by 1–3 days.
- Model often fails to account for sentiment momentum — if sentiment is trending upward, reduce forecast lag by 1–2 days.
- When sentiment is mixed (±0.3), model tends to overfit recent history — smooth forecast by 1–2% downward for 3–5 days.
- Model underestimates true volatility in sentiment-driven corrections — increase forecast variance by 1–3% for 2–4 days.
